chapters.title: Chapter 4: Industrial Metals and Global Growth

lessons.title: China's Demand Footprint and Global Supply Chains

children.text: China Is Not Just the Biggest Buyer. It's Also the Biggest Maker

The previous lesson flagged China repeatedly as the single biggest swing factor for copper and steel demand. That is only half the story. China is also the world's largest producer of steel and one of the dominant processors of the critical minerals that feed electronics and battery supply chains. This dual role, biggest buyer and biggest maker at once, is what makes Chinese policy decisions move global metal markets from both directions simultaneously, sometimes in ways that pull against each other.

body.text: When analysts say 'watch China' for metals, they don't just mean China is buying. They mean China's own factories and mills are a huge share of the world's supply too, which is why one country's policy can move a global price from two directions at once.

body.label: China's Share of Global Crude Steel Production
body.context: China has produced around half of the world's crude steel for well over a decade, a remarkably stable share even as its own domestic demand growth has slowed.

children.text: This dual role has a direct consequence for how you should read Chinese news. A property slowdown in China cuts Chinese steel demand, which sounds unambiguously bearish for steel prices. But if the same slowdown pushes Beijing to order production curbs at Chinese steel mills, whether for pollution control, overcapacity management, or ahead of a major diplomatic event, that cuts global supply at the same time. The two effects pull in opposite directions, and which one dominates the actual price move is genuinely ambiguous until you look at the numbers.
How to Actually Track the China Signal
You do not need to read Mandarin-language economic reports to track China's demand pulse. A handful of monthly data points, all covered in English-language financial media, do most of the work.
Manufacturing PMI (both the official NBS PMI and the private Caixin PMI): a reading above 50 signals expansion, below 50 signals contraction in factory activity
Property and real estate investment growth: the most direct read on steel and construction-linked metal demand
Total Social Financing and new yuan loan data: a proxy for how much credit is flowing into the economy, which tends to lead construction and industrial activity by a few months
China's own commodity import volumes: reported monthly, and often a more reliable real-time read than sentiment-based surveys
The Property Slowdown vs the New Economy Offset

events.title: The 'Three Red Lines' Policy
events.description: Beijing introduced strict leverage limits on property developers, deliberately tightening credit to an overheated sector that had been a major driver of steel and copper demand for two decades.

events.title: The Evergrande Default
events.description: One of China's largest property developers defaulted on its debt, triggering a broader crisis of confidence in the property sector that has weighed on construction-linked metals demand for years since.

events.title: A Structural Property Drag, Partly Offset by EVs
events.description: Property investment stayed weak through this period, dragging on steel and, to a lesser extent, copper demand. At the same time, China became the world's largest electric vehicle market, and its EV and battery supply chain buildout provided a meaningful offset to copper and battery-metal demand even as the old construction-led growth model faded.

children.text: China's Grip on Critical Mineral Processing

China's dominance goes beyond steel and refined copper. It also processes a large majority of the world's rare earth elements and refines a significant majority of the world's lithium, both critical inputs into the EV and renewable energy supply chains that are increasingly important demand drivers for the metals covered in this course.

stats.label: China's Share of Global Rare Earth Processing
stats.context: Widely cited estimate from international energy agencies; the exact figure moves as other countries build out processing capacity

stats.label: China's Share of Global Lithium Refining
stats.context: Even where the raw ore is mined elsewhere, most of it is still sent to China to be refined into battery-grade material

children.text: The 'China Plus One' Shift, and India's Opening

Since the pandemic, global manufacturers have increasingly looked to diversify supply chains away from sole reliance on China, a trend often shorthanded as 'China Plus One'. India has tried to position itself as a beneficiary through schemes like the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme, which includes a dedicated push for domestic specialty steel manufacturing alongside electronics and other sectors.

body.text: Treat 'China Plus One' as a real, ongoing structural trend rather than a completed shift. China's share of global manufacturing and metal processing remains dominant today, and diversification of this scale plays out over many years, not quarters. It is a theme worth watching for how India's metals sector evolves, not a reason to assume China's influence on these cycles is fading quickly.

body.title: Untangle the Dual Role
body.scenario: China reports weak property investment data for the month, a clearly demand-negative signal for steel. In the same week, Beijing also announces steel mill production curbs ahead of a major international summit, a supply-negative signal.
body.prompt: Why can the net effect on global steel prices be genuinely ambiguous here, rather than obviously bearish?
body.modelAnswer: Both news items originate from China, but they push in opposite directions. Weak property data signals lower Chinese steel demand, which on its own would be bearish for price. But production curbs simultaneously remove supply from the market, which is bullish for price on its own. Because both effects are real and both are happening in China at the same time, the net direction for global steel prices depends on which effect is larger in magnitude and how the market weighs the curbs' likely duration against the demand data's likely persistence. This is exactly the kind of situation where reacting to a single headline, without asking whether it's a demand story or a supply story, leads to the wrong conclusion.

points: China is both the world's largest metals consumer and, for steel especially, roughly half of global production, which means Chinese policy can move prices from the demand side and the supply side at once, sometimes in opposite directions.
Track the China signal through a handful of monthly data points: manufacturing PMI, property investment growth, credit and Total Social Financing data, and China's own commodity import volumes.

China's property sector has been in a structural slowdown since the 2020 'three red lines' policy and the 2021 Evergrande default, a drag on steel and construction-linked metal demand that China's EV and renewables buildout has only partly offset.

China's dominance extends beyond the metals in this course to critical mineral processing, roughly 85% of rare earths and around two-thirds of lithium refining, which underpins the EV and grid demand that is reshaping copper and aluminium consumption.

The 'China Plus One' supply chain diversification trend is real and relevant to India's own manufacturing ambitions, including specialty steel, but it remains an early-stage, multi-year shift rather than a fait accompli.
